defs_parts: Seven labels sit in the corners of the pictures that follow.
In the book text: the course text uses and explains the term.
In the glossary: the term is on the course term list, but the text does not explain it.
Video only: the term comes from a video lecture, and is not in the course text or on the term list.
Computed: the numbers are worked out on screen from stated inputs.
Simulation: a model run step by step from stated rules, not a measurement of a real game.
Illustrative data: numbers chosen to show the idea, not measured.
Conceptual: a drawing of the idea, with no data behind it.
recap_lines: A game needs a goal, opposition, decisions and rules, all four of them.
A house rule is still a rule, one group's own change to the rules.
The core mechanic is the action repeated most, and the core loop is the cycle.
What a thing does, and how it moves, tells the player what it is.
Name one target experience, because plain fun is too vague to build or test.
A prototype tests the idea, and play testing refines the design round by round.
bookends.command: Quiz me on game design terms with short game-making cases, one at a time. Use goal, opposition, decisions, house rules, mechanic, component, core mechanic, core loop, target experience and play testing. For each case I must name the exact term and say why its look-alike does not fit. Hold back the answer until I reply, then tell me whether I was right.
checks: Check: every case is about making a game, and the answer waits for you.
Check: you named the exact term and said why its look-alike does not fit.
